claims.text: In a field test across 191 countries, an explicitly gender-neutral STEM career ad was displayed to over 20% more men than women.
Conditional on seeing the STEM career ad, women were significantly more likely to click on the ad than men.
Country-level measures of female labor market participation, female education, and general gender equality are not significantly related to the gender disparity in STEM ad delivery.
Female demographic groups, particularly women aged 25–44, have higher suggested bidding prices on social media ad auctions than male demographic groups.
Conditional on clicking an ad, women are more likely to convert by adding products to their shopping cart than men in an e-commerce context.
The pattern of delivering more STEM ad impressions to men than women generalizes across Google Display Network, Instagram, and Twitter.

evidence.description: Empirically, across 191 countries on Facebook, the STEM career ad was shown to over 20% more men than women, with the disparity most pronounced in the 25-54 age range.
Across all campaigns, the aggregate average click-rate for men was 0.131% compared to 0.167% for women (p < 0.001), and logit regression confirms positive coefficients for Female on click propensity.

Interactions between female indicator and World Bank high-equality metrics (labor participation, primary/secondary education, CPIA gender equality index) yielded statistically insignificant coefficients in regression models of ad reach.

On average, the ad platform suggested bidding about 5 cents more to advertise to women (p < 0.05), with women aged 25-34 being 17.4 cents higher (p < 0.1) and women aged 35-44 being 15.0 cents higher (p < 0.001).
In campaign data from an online fashion/household retailer, women were consistently more likely than men to add products to their shopping cart after clicking on an ad across age groups.

Google Display Network showed 38,000 male vs 26,817 female impressions (51% vs 36%); Instagram showed 9,595 male vs 1,560 female impressions; Twitter spent $46.84 on men (66,243 impressions) vs $31 on women (52,363 impressions).

methodologies.name: Cross-national Field Test on Facebook
methodologies.description: Executed identical ad campaigns promoting STEM career opportunities across 191 countries targeted at all adults aged 18+ to observe algorithmically determined impression distribution, reach, and clickthrough rates across age and gender.
conditions: Initial max bid $0.20/click (raised up to $0.60 in 29 countries)

methodologies.name: Cross-Platform US Replication Field Tests
methodologies.description: Deployed gender-neutral STEM career advertisements on Google Display Network, Instagram, and Twitter in the US market without gender targeting restrictions to analyze impression and cost metrics across platforms.

methodologies.name: Retail Conversion and Pricing Analysis
methodologies.description: Analyzed demographic-specific ad pricing suggestions from Facebook and e-commerce conversion data from an online fashion/household goods retailer to assess economic valuations of male vs female demographics.
conditions: Identical retail campaigns targeted separately by age and gender in US

limitations.text: The primary field test consists of a single ad design for STEM careers shown across multiple countries.
Because the internal mechanics of the ad delivery algorithm are unobserved, results regarding the precise role of bidding decisions by other advertisers remain suggestive rather than conclusive.
The study cannot directly test the extent to which ad algorithms themselves may contain intrinsic non-economic biases.
The study's results are descriptive and explain an empirical regularity without empirically testing policy intervention measures that could prevent discriminatory ad delivery outcomes.
Prior literature on algorithmic bias in advertising documents discriminatory empirical patterns without empirically examining the underlying causal mechanisms within the ad ecosystem.

future_work.text: Testing specific policy prescriptions and platform feature mechanisms (such as allowing advertisers to automatically equalize impression distribution across demographic groups) to prevent cost-optimization algorithms from generating demographic imbalances.
